items.stem: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
options: They have the same specific heat capacity
They have the same internal energy
There is no net transfer of thermal energy between them
They contain the same amount of thermal energy
items.answer: There is no net transfer of thermal energy between them
items.markingKey: Thermal equilibrium means equal temperatures, so no net energy flow.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by thermal equilibrium and why a thermometer must be in thermal equilibrium with an object to measure its temperature.
items.answer: Thermal equilibrium: no net transfer of thermal energy between bodies in contact because they are at the same temperature. The thermometer reads its own temperature, which equals the object's only when there is no net energy flow.
items.markingKey: no net energy transfer / same temperature [1]; thermometer reads own temperature, equal only at equilibrium [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why temperature, not internal energy, determines the direction of thermal energy transfer.
items.answer: A large cool object may have more internal energy than a small hot one, but energy still flows from hot to cold; net flow depends on temperature (mean random kinetic energy of particles), not total energy.
items.markingKey: counter-example of large cool object [1]; flow from higher to lower temperature [1] [2]

items.stem: In a data book, a freezer is set to −18 °C. Work out the thermodynamic temperature.
items.markingKey: T = θ + 273.15 = −18 + 273.15 = 255.2 K. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sample is warmed from 464 °C to 504 °C. Calculate the initial and final thermodynamic temperatures and the temperature rise in kelvin.

A technician in Santiago calibrates a freezer thermometer. (a) Convert 15 °C to kelvin. (b) State the significance of the temperature 0 K. (c) Explain why a temperature change of 10 °C equals a change of 10 K.
items.answer: (a) 288.2 K (b) Absolute zero: the internal energy of a substance is a minimum. (c) The kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size; the scales only differ in their zero.
items.markingKey: (a) T = θ + 273.15: 288.2 K [1] (b) Absolute zero: the internal energy of a substance is a minimum [1] (c) same size of degree [1]; offset of 273.15 [1] [2]

items.stem: What is 27 °C on the thermodynamic temperature scale?

Answer both parts. (a) State the equation linking thermodynamic temperature T in kelvin and Celsius temperature θ. (b) Thermal energy is transferred between two objects in contact. Which property determines the direction of the net transfer?
items.answer: (a) T/K = θ/°C + 273.15 (b) temperature
items.markingKey: (a) T = θ + 273.15 [1] (b) Net energy flows from higher to lower temperature.

items.stem: Explain why scales based on different thermometric properties may give different readings between the fixed points.
items.answer: Each scale is defined to agree at the fixed points, but the properties (e.g. resistance, e.m.f., expansion) do not vary linearly in the same way with temperature, so readings in between can differ.
items.markingKey: agree at fixed points by definition [1]; properties not linear in the same way [1] [2]

items.stem: State what is meant by absolute zero and explain why there is no temperature lower than it.
items.answer: Absolute zero (0 K) is the temperature at which a substance has minimum internal energy; energy cannot be removed below the minimum, so no lower temperature exists.
items.markingKey: minimum internal energy [1]; cannot be lower [1] [2]

items.stem: A hot rivet at 400 °C is placed in contact with a large steel girder at 20 °C. A student says thermal energy will flow into the hotter object because the other has more internal energy. Explain why the student is wrong and describe what happens until thermal equilibrium is reached.
items.answer: Net thermal energy flows from higher to lower temperature, i.e. from a hot rivet at 400 °C to a large steel girder at 20 °C, regardless of internal energy, until both reach the same temperature, after which there is no net transfer.
items.markingKey: direction set by temperature not internal energy [1]; flow from hotter to colder [1]; continues until same temperature, then no net transfer [1] [3]

items.stem: A small copper coin at 60 °C is placed in contact with a bucket of sand at 25 °C. A student says thermal energy will flow into the hotter object because the other has more internal energy. Explain why the student is wrong and describe what happens until thermal equilibrium is reached.
items.answer: Net thermal energy flows from higher to lower temperature, i.e. from a small copper coin at 60 °C to a bucket of sand at 25 °C, regardless of internal energy, until both reach the same temperature, after which there is no net transfer.
items.markingKey: direction set by temperature not internal energy [1]; flow from hotter to colder [1]; continues until same temperature, then no net transfer [1] [3]

items.stem: A weather station in Riyadh records temperatures on both scales. (a) State what is meant by thermal equilibrium. (b) Explain why the thermodynamic scale is called an absolute scale. (c) State the significance of the temperature 0 K. (d) Explain why a temperature change of 10 °C equals a change of 10 K.
items.answer: (a) No net transfer of thermal energy between two bodies (they are at the same temperature). (b) It does not depend on the property of any substance and its zero is absolute zero. (c) Absolute zero: the internal energy of a substance is a minimum. (d) The kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size; the scales only differ in their zero.

items.stem: Which physical property is used in a thermocouple thermometer?
options: the pressure of a fixed volume of gas
the e.m.f. produced at a junction of two different metals
items.answer: the e.m.f. produced at a junction of two different metals
items.markingKey: A thermocouple e.m.f. depends on the temperature difference between junctions.

items.stem: What is an advantage of a thermocouple compared with a liquid-in-glass thermometer?
options: it is accurate only near room temperature
it has a small heat capacity and responds quickly
it has a perfectly linear scale
items.answer: it has a small heat capacity and responds quickly
items.markingKey: Small junction: fast response, wide range, remote reading.

items.stem: Compare a thermistor and a thermocouple as thermometers for monitoring the temperature of a kiln and of a baby's bath.
items.answer: Kiln: thermocouple, because of its very wide range (hundreds of °C) and robustness. Bath: thermistor, because it is very sensitive over a narrow range near 37 °C.
items.markingKey: thermocouple for kiln with reason (range) [1]; thermistor for bath with reason (sensitivity) [1] [2]

items.stem: Elena uses the resistance of a platinum wire as a thermometric property. Its value is 100 Ω at 0 °C and 138.5 Ω at 100 °C. At an unknown temperature it is 115 Ω. Calculate the unknown temperature on this scale.
items.markingKey: θ = (115 − 100)/(138.5 − 100) × 100 = 39.0 °C. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A thermistor has a resistance of 5.0 kΩ at 0 °C and 0.35 kΩ at 100 °C. When placed in a liquid its resistance is 1.2 kΩ. (a) State what type of thermistor this is and explain how you know. (b) Explain why the true temperature may differ from this value. (c) State one advantage of a thermocouple over a thermistor.
items.answer: (a) NTC: resistance decreases as temperature increases. (b) Thermistor resistance does not vary linearly with temperature (it is roughly exponential). (c) Much wider range / smaller with faster response / measures at a point.
items.markingKey: (a) NTC: resistance decreases as temperature increases [1] (b) Thermistor resistance does not vary linearly with temperature (it is roughly exponential) [1] (c) Much wider range / smaller with faster response / measures at a point [1]

items.stem: The resistance of an NTC thermistor …
items.answer: decreases as temperature increases
items.markingKey: More charge carriers are released as temperature rises.

items.stem: Explain why a thermistor thermometer and a resistance-wire thermometer, both calibrated at 0 °C and 100 °C, may disagree at 50 °C.
items.answer: Each reading assumes resistance varies linearly between fixed points; the thermistor's resistance varies non-linearly (roughly exponentially) and differently from the metal's, so interpolated values differ.
items.markingKey: scales agree only at fixed points [1]; non-linear/different variation [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a thermocouple can measure the temperature at a point.
items.answer: The junction is very small, so it has a low heat capacity and measures the temperature at that point quickly without disturbing it much.
items.markingKey: small junction [1]; low heat capacity / quick response [1] [2]

items.stem: Suggest why the e.m.f. of a thermocouple must be measured with a high-resistance voltmeter.
items.answer: Thermocouple e.m.f.s are small (millivolts) and the source may have internal resistance; a high-resistance meter draws little current, so the p.d. measured is close to the e.m.f.
items.markingKey: small e.m.f. [1]; little current drawn so reading ≈ e.m.f. [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas uses the e.m.f. of a thermocouple (one junction in melting ice) as a thermometric property. Its value is 0 mV at 0 °C and 4.1 mV at 100 °C. At an unknown temperature it is 3.3 mV. Determine the unknown temperature on this scale.
items.markingKey: θ = (3.3 − 0)/(4.1 − 0) × 100 = 80.5 °C. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Sipho uses the length of a liquid thread in a capillary as a thermometric property. Its value is 25 mm at 0 °C and 205 mm at 100 °C. At an unknown temperature it is 170 mm. Calculate the unknown temperature on this scale.
items.markingKey: θ = (170 − 25)/(205 − 25) × 100 = 80.6 °C. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Samuel uses the resistance of a platinum wire as a thermometric property. Its value is 100 Ω at 0 °C and 138.5 Ω at 100 °C. At an unknown temperature it is 130 Ω. Calculate the unknown temperature on this scale and state the assumption made.
items.answer: 77.9 °C; assumes R varies linearly with temperature
items.markingKey: θ = (R − R₀)/(R₁₀₀ − R₀) × 100 [1]; = 77.9 °C [1]; linear variation assumed [1] [3]

items.stem: Arjun uses the resistance of a metal-film sensor as a thermometric property. Its value is 500 Ω at 0 °C and 690 Ω at 100 °C. At an unknown temperature it is 540 Ω. (a) Calculate the unknown temperature on this scale. (b) Convert it to kelvin. (c) A gas thermometer gives a slightly different reading at this temperature. Explain why.
items.answer: (a) 21.1 °C (b) 294.2 K (c) the two properties do not vary linearly with temperature in the same way; scales only agree at the fixed points

items.stem: A thermistor has a resistance of 3.5 kΩ at 0 °C and 0.60 kΩ at 100 °C. When placed in a liquid its resistance is 1.5 kΩ. (a) Assuming the resistance varies linearly with temperature, calculate the temperature of the liquid. (b) State one advantage of a thermistor over a thermocouple. (c) State one advantage of a thermocouple over a thermistor.

items.stem: Which is the definition of specific heat capacity?
options: the energy required per unit mass to raise the temperature by one kelvin
the energy required to raise the temperature of an object by 1 K
the energy required per unit mass to change state
the energy stored per kelvin in an object
items.answer: the energy required per unit mass to raise the temperature by one kelvin
items.markingKey: c = E/(mΔθ).

items.stem: Explain why a block of metal being heated electrically should be well insulated when measuring its specific heat capacity.
items.answer: Thermal energy is lost to the surroundings, so not all the electrical energy VIt raises the temperature; the value of c calculated would be too large. Insulation reduces these losses.
items.markingKey: energy lost to surroundings [1]; calculated c too high, insulation reduces losses [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the temperature of a substance stays constant while it boils.
items.answer: The energy supplied is used to break intermolecular bonds and separate the molecules (increase in potential energy) and do work against the atmosphere; the mean kinetic energy, and hence temperature, does not change.
items.markingKey: energy breaks bonds / increases PE [1]; mean KE (temperature) unchanged [1] [2]

items.stem: An electrical heater connected to a 24 V supply passes a current of 2.5 A. It heats a 0.50 kg block of concrete for 420 s, and the temperature rises by 57.3 K. Energy losses are negligible. Calculate the specific heat capacity of concrete.
items.answer: 880 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
items.markingKey: c = VIt/(mΔθ) = 24 × 2.5 × 420/(0.50 × 57.3) = 880 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An electrical heater connected to a 12 V supply passes a current of 5.0 A. It heats a 0.50 kg block of concrete for 300 s, and the temperature rises by 40.9 K. Energy losses are negligible. Calculate the energy supplied and the specific heat capacity of concrete.
items.answer: E = 18 000 J; c = 880 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹

items.stem: An electrical heater connected to a 12 V supply passes a current of 4.5 A. It heats a 0.80 kg block of iron for 300 s, and the temperature rises by 45 K. (a) Calculate the energy supplied by the heater. (b) Calculate a value for the specific heat capacity, assuming no losses. (c) In fact 15% of the energy is lost to the surroundings. Calculate the corrected value and explain whether the first value was too high or too low.

items.stem: A 1.0 kg block of aluminium is heated by a 60 W heater inserted in a hole in the block. A thermometer is placed in a second hole. (a) Define specific heat capacity. (b) Describe how the heater power would be measured. (c) Explain why the measured rate of temperature rise is less than the calculated value.
items.answer: (a) Energy per unit mass needed to raise the temperature by 1 K. (b) Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with the heater; P = VI. (c) Energy is lost to the surroundings and used to heat the heater and thermometer.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy per unit mass needed to raise the temperature by 1 K [1] (b) ammeter and voltmeter [1]; P = VI [1] [2] (c) Energy is lost to the surroundings and used to heat the heater and thermometer [1]

(b) The specific heat capacity of brass is 380 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the rate of rise of temperature in K per minute, assuming no losses. (c) Describe how the heater power would be measured.
items.answer: (a) Energy per unit mass needed to raise the temperature by 1 K. (b) 3.95 K min⁻¹ (c) Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with the heater; P = VI.

items.stem: What is the unit of specific latent heat?
items.answer: J kg⁻¹

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which is the definition of specific heat capacity? (b) During melting at constant temperature, the energy supplied mainly …
items.answer: (a) the energy required per unit mass to raise the temperature by one kelvin (b) increases the potential energy of the molecules
items.markingKey: (a) c = E/(mΔθ). (b) Bonds are broken; mean kinetic energy stays constant.

items.stem: Explain how using two different heater powers allows energy losses to be eliminated when measuring specific latent heat of vaporisation.
items.answer: With the liquid boiling steadily at the same temperature, the rate of heat loss h is the same in both runs: P₁t = m₁L + ht and P₂t = m₂L + ht. Subtracting eliminates h: L = (P₁ − P₂)t/(m₁ − m₂).
items.markingKey: heat loss rate same in both runs (same temperature) [1]; subtract equations to eliminate loss [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a heater should be left on for several minutes before readings are taken in a latent heat experiment.
items.answer: The apparatus must reach a steady state (boiling steadily, constant temperature), so that the rate of energy loss is constant and all supplied energy goes into the change of state plus a steady loss.
items.markingKey: steady state reached [1]; constant loss rate [1] [2]

items.stem: What is absolute zero on the Celsius scale?

Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain what is meant by thermal equilibrium and why a thermometer must be in thermal equilibrium with an object to measure its temperature. (b) Explain why temperature, not internal energy, determines the direction of thermal energy transfer.
items.answer: (a) Thermal equilibrium: no net transfer of thermal energy between bodies in contact because they are at the same temperature. The thermometer reads its own temperature, which equals the object's only when there is no net energy flow. (b) A large cool object may have more internal energy than a small hot one, but energy still flows from hot to cold; net flow depends on temperature (mean random kinetic energy of particles), not total energy.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a heater should be left on for several minutes before readings are taken in a latent heat experiment. (b) Explain how using two different heater powers allows energy losses to be eliminated when measuring specific latent heat of vaporisation.
items.answer: (a) The apparatus must reach a steady state (boiling steadily, constant temperature), so that the rate of energy loss is constant and all supplied energy goes into the change of state plus a steady loss. (b) With the liquid boiling steadily at the same temperature, the rate of heat loss h is the same in both runs: P₁t = m₁L + ht and P₂t = m₂L + ht. Subtracting eliminates h: L = (P₁ − P₂)t/(m₁ − m₂).
items.markingKey: (a) steady state reached [1]; constant loss rate [1] [2] (b) heat loss rate same in both runs (same temperature) [1]; subtract equations to eliminate loss [1] [2]
